sentences: This is Utagawa Hiroshige's Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake.
On a summer afternoon, a sudden shower pours down on a great bridge in Edo, and the whole tall sheet is veiled in slanting rain.
The print is number 58 in the series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo and was published in the ninth month of 1857, near the end of Hiroshige's life.
Many impressions were pulled from the same blocks, so museums around the world hold copies.
At the very top, dark cloud fades downward in a soft gradation.
This is bokashi, made by grading the ink on the woodblock, so the clouds vary noticeably from one impression to the next, and no two skies are quite alike.
At the upper right, a red strip carries the series title, and the patterned panel beside it names this particular view.
They are small, but they work like signposts within the print.
Even through the rain, these coloured panels stay crisp.
Now look at the rain itself.
Hiroshige had it cut as dense, fine lines running in two slightly different directions.
The two layers cross, and the downpour seems to shift and sway in the gusting wind.
The far bank dissolves into soft grey shapes behind the rain.
That is Atake, named after the shogunate's great ship Atakemaru, which was once moored there.
The river beneath the bridge is the Sumida.
On the river, a lone raftsman poles his long log raft along, carrying on through the rain as if nothing were happening at all.
He is described as heading for the timber yards of Fukagawa.
On the bridge, people hurry across under straw hats, umbrellas and matting held over their heads: two women and four or five men.
Their hunched postures and quick little steps alone tell us how heavy the rain is.
The bridge enters on a steep diagonal, cropped at both ends and seen as if from above.
It was a daring composition for its time, and the heavy wooden piers give the whole scene a firm, steady rhythm.
Thirty years later, in 1887, Van Gogh copied this woodblock print in oils in Paris.
He made the colours more intense than the original and framed his copy with a border of Japanese characters he borrowed from other prints.
Step back and look at the whole sheet again.
A few layers of fine lines are enough to make the air feel this wet.
Listen closely: can you almost hear the rain drumming on the wooden planks of the bridge?
